claim_boundary.supports: For EVERY rational point z = (x, y) of the unit circle (kernel-checked): z has finite order iff z is one of (1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), (0,-1), i.e. the torsion of the unit Gaussian rationals is exactly mu_4; if 2x is not an integer the point has infinite order (integer sequence W_n = c^n 2 Re z^n with W_{n+2} = a W_{n+1} - c^2 W_n is a^n modulo a prime p dividing c, while z^n = 1 would give 2 c^n); x = +-1/2 is impossible (y^2 = 3/4 has no rational root), so there is no order-3 or order-6 phase and every finite phase group inside the Gaussian rationals has exponent dividing 4; the Cayley map (m, n) -> ((n^2 - m^2)/(n^2 + m^2), 2mn/(n^2 + m^2)) lands on the circle (cayley_on_circle) and every point with x != -1 equals Cayley(m, n) for (m, n) = (y, 1 + x) (every_point_is_cayley); (-1, 0) is also reached, at n = 0 (cayley_reaches_south_pole), so the map is onto the circle; the Cayley points include the four points of mu_4; the infinite-order rational points are exactly those with 2x not an integer, i.e. the circle minus mu_4; (3/5, 4/5) has infinite order (u345_infinite_order, the kernel instance). Native (exact enumeration, not kernel theorems): the exhaustive list of the five cases 2x = -2..2 (two refused at x = +-1/2); 15 Cayley points with the smallest prime p dividing den(2x) and the valuation law v_p(2 Re z^k) = -k v_p(den 2x) for k = 1..6; orders are searched up to 12, so order 0 means "no power equal to 1 up to 12" and infinite order itself rests on the kernel theorem; two census rows (B = 3 and 6: 16 and 48 distinct Cayley points, exactly 4 in mu_4, (-1,0) reached); and a finite-field table: the unit circle over F_p has p-1 points for p = 1 mod 4, p+1 for p = 3 mod 4 and is cyclic, so phases of orders beyond 4 occur there (13 primes up to 43, brute force).
claim_boundary.does_not_support: Any derivation of C or U(1) from finite carriers, or a proof that no such derivation exists: the node is a pointer to QM_028 / QM_062 owned by another segment and its selection is NOT established here; finite carriers in the sense of finite fields or finite rings (the unit circle over F_p has order p -+ 1, native table only): the theorem is a no-go only for finite subgroups of the unit Gaussian rationals, and the identification of a finite phase carrier with such a subgroup is not argued; larger finite phase groups in cyclotomic extensions (Q(zeta_8), Q(zeta_3), ...) which this result does not treat; completion, continuity, compactness or Haar measure of the circle; that there are infinitely many infinite-order points as a kernel statement (only the instance u345_infinite_order and the native census); the rival split-complex hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 (the H011 flag rival_excluded); the H011 selector pack, whose selector_not_free is rfl on a record with a hand-set Boolean field; any physical reading of phases.
claim_boundary.narrowest_claim: Inside the unit Gaussian rationals the only phases of finite order are the four elements of mu_4; the rational circle points outside mu_4 are exactly those with 2x not an integer and they have infinite order (kernel instance: (3/5, 4/5)), so a finite phase group inside the Gaussian rationals has order dividing 4, whereas the unit circle over a finite field F_p is a different finite carrier with p -+ 1 elements (native table, not a kernel statement).
claim_boundary.next_test: Determine the unit circle {x^2 + y^2 = 1} over F_p and over Z/n exactly: prove that it is cyclic of order p - (-1/p) and show which phase orders a finite scalar ring does and does not force, as the finite-carrier counterpart of the Gaussian-rational torsion result; the torsion over Q(i, sqrt 2) and Q(zeta_3) is a secondary item.

earlier_pass.notes: I recompiled lean4/U1SelectorSegment.lean (Lean 4.35.0, exit 0, all 13 anchors on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound only); p1 construction copies are byte-identical to production. The core theorem is real and correctly stated: circle_torsion / circle_torsion_iff say that for every rational (x,y) with x^2+y^2=1, z^n=1 for some n>0 iff z is in mu_4, via not_torsion_of_den (2x not an integer implies z^n != 1 for all n>0, with the W_n recurrence reduced mod a prime p | den(2x), p not dividing the numerator, since the fraction is reduced), circle_integral_case (2x integer: k in -2..2, k = +-1 excluded by no_point_with_x_half), torsion_exponent_divides_four, cube_root_trivial. I found no gap in that chain. Mathematically this is the classical fact that the roots of unity in Q(i) are mu_4, reproved elementarily; the profile does not claim novelty, fine. DEFECT IN THE CLAIM TEXT (Cayley). supports says the Cayley map 'reaches every point except (-1, 0)', the Lean module docstring says 'the infinite-order points are exactly the rest of the circle (every point except (-1,0))', and narrowest_claim says 'the infinitely many other rational circle points (all Cayley points) are not finite-carrier phases'. All three are false or misleading. every_point_is_cayley only proves that every point with x != -1 is in the image of (m,n) -> ((n^2-m^2)/(n^2+m^2), 2mn/(n^2+m^2)) (take m = y, n = 1 + x); it does not say (-1,0) is missed, and it is not missed: n = 0, m != 0 gives (-1,0), so the image is the whole circle. And Cayley points include mu_4: (m,n)=(0,1)->(1,0), (1,0)->(-1,0), (1,1)->(0,1)=i, (-1,1)->(0,-1); the certificate's own records show orders 1, 2, 4, 4 for them. The infinite-order points are exactly those with 2x not an integer, i.e. the circle minus mu_4, not 'all Cayley points'. 'Infinitely many' is not backed by an anchor either (only u345_infinite_order, a single instance; the certificate has 15 points). The Lean docstring itself contains the wrong sentence, so fixing it changes a pinned source file. OTHER OVERREACH. (a) The node is the pointer 'Selection of C and U(1) from finite carriers'. The theorem is about a finite SUBGROUP of the unit Gaussian rationals. The bridge 'finite carrier = finite subgroup of Q(i)^x' is not argued: finite carriers in the usual sense (finite fields F_q) have unit circles of order q -+ 1, i.e. finite phase groups of orders other than 1, 2, 4. The result is a no-go for finite phase carriers inside Q(i) only; does_not_support names cyclotomic extensions but not finite fields/other finite scalar rings, which is the more obvious reading of 'finite carrier'. (b) next_test (torsion over Q(i,sqrt2) is mu_8, over Q(zeta_3) mu_12) is a refinement of the 'cyclotomic extensions not treated' clause of does_not_support rather than the node's own unpaid obligation (selecting C/U(1) from finite carriers); it is acceptable as a next step but not independent of does_not_support. Better: decide the torsion of the unit circle over finite fields F_p (orders p -+ 1) and over Z/n, to show what a genuinely finite carrier selects. CHECKER. Independent of the producer's recurrence: it writes z = A/d with A a Gaussian integer, computes A^k by exact Gaussian multiplication, reads the order from A^n == d^n for n <= 12, computes v_p(2 Re A^k) - k v_p(d), and verifies the valuation law v = -k v_p(den 2x) and 'order == 0' on every non-integral point (theorem-level, not assumed), and 'order in {1,2,4}' for integral 2x. The half cases use P*Q squareness (producer tests numerator and denominator separately). All leaves are compared with exact types. Caveat: order = 0 means 'no power equal to 1 up to 12', so the certificate itself only shows 'not torsion up to 12' and relies on the kernel for infinite order; the profile phrase 'exact orders' should be read with that. Caveat: only the smallest prime dividing den(2x) is tested; a second prime is not exercised, though the law holds for any. MUTANTS. sixth_root_of_unity and valuation_exponent_off_by_one/wrong_prime are real near misses to stated bridges (no x = 1/2 point; v_5 exponent 2 for den 25 versus v_13 with exponent 2 for den 169 at (5,12)); pythagorean_point_is_a_quarter_turn, unit_i_has_infinite_order, identity_read_as_minus_one, search_bound_read_as_order, non_unit_point_flagged_as_mu4, integral_twice_x_for_a_cayley_point are flipped fields. Missing near misses: (a) 'every Cayley point has infinite order' (the profile's own error; unit_i_has_infinite_order is the field version but the intended error is generalisation); (b) 'the Cayley map misses (-1,0)'; (c) 'infinitely many torsion-free points' presented without an anchor; (d) a finite-field circle with order p+1 read as contradicting the result (scope near miss). DAG: the node is a pointer, labelled PROVED_LEAN on the strength of fixed-instance Layer 1-3 bookkeeping; the new result does not discharge the pointer statement. I would lower the status to a pointer/source-record level and attach the torsion fact as a scoped, separate result.
